title: Plants can speak using electricity, so this startup built an AI model to decipher their language
slides: Plants 'speak' via electrical signals—but what are they saying?
A startup built an AI to decode these plant signals.
The AI predicts stress from voltage patterns, not chemicals.
Farmers could get early warnings for crop stress.
Test this: ask if your farm's plants are sending distress signals.
thread_text:
1. Your crops are screaming

A startup's AI reads voltage spikes in plant tissue to predict stress hours before visible damage. The signals are electrical, not chemical.

2. Voltage, not chemistry

Most plant diagnostics look for hormones or metabolites. This model skips the molecules and goes straight to the electrical patterns—faster and cheaper to capture.

3. Early warning, no lab

Farmers could get alerts from a field sensor before leaves wilt. That gap between signal and symptom is where interventions still work.

4. The language problem

We can detect distress, but we can't yet read specific causes. Is it drought, pests, or disease? The AI flags stress without naming it.

5. Test it on your farm

Ask your agronomist if any local pilot is collecting electrical plant data. If not, request a trial—and see what your fields are saying.

Your crops send electrical voltage spikes when they're stressed — hours before you can see any damage.

A startup built an AI that reads those voltage patterns instead of hormones or metabolites. Faster and cheaper to capture, no lab needed.

A field sensor could alert farmers before leaves wilt — the gap where intervention still works.

One catch: the AI flags stress but can't say if it's drought, pests, or disease. ⚡
